hook: In 2016, UK voters chose to leave the European Union to "take back control." In 1999, Canada created Nunavut so that Inuit could govern their own territory. In 1991, the Soviet Union broke into 15 states. Sovereignty can be shared upward, to groups of states, and downward, to regions, and both change what a national government can decide alone.

options: Moving power from the national government to regions
Moving power from regions to the national government
A state taking land where its people live
A state's right and power to govern its territory without outside control

figure.caption: Sovereignty can be shared upward to supranational organizations and downward to regions.

chain.cause: Some problems cross borders, such as defense, disease, pollution and trade
chain.effect: states join supranational organizations to face them together

chain.cause: Members agree to shared rules, courts or decisions
chain.effect: each state gives up some sovereignty in return for the gains

chain.cause: Regions demand more self-rule at the same time
chain.effect: power also moves down to autonomous regions, or a state breaks apart

ideas: Devolution can create autonomous regions or subnational units (Spain, Belgium, Canada's Nunavut, Nigeria's states) or break a state apart (Sudan in 2011, the Soviet Union in 1991). Balkanization is a breakup into smaller, often hostile states.
Supranationalism is cooperation among three or more states through an organization: the UN, NATO, the EU, ASEAN, the African Union, the Arctic Council. Members give up some sovereignty.
Communication technology can help devolution, supranational cooperation and democratization, the spread of democratic government.

misconception.wrong: Every supranational organization limits its members in the same way.
misconception.right: Organizations differ by function. EU members follow shared laws and court rulings; NATO members pledge shared defense; the Arctic Council acts only when all eight states agree, so it limits sovereignty little.

summary: Sovereignty is challenged from below and above. Devolution can create autonomous regions and subnational units, as in Spain, Belgium, Canada and Nigeria, or break a state apart, as with Sudan and the Soviet Union. Supranational organizations such as the UN, NATO, the EU, ASEAN, the African Union and the Arctic Council help states face shared problems, gain larger markets and defend each other, but limit what each member decides alone. Communication technology speeds all of these changes, including democratization.
